title: Republicans’ wipeout a vote on AI insurgence
full_text:
In the fallout from Donald Trump’s midterm repudiation, an issue stands out – the Democratic Party-led purge of Trump’s runaway support for AI and Big Tech that signals a US shift to more political accountability in the management of AI and data centres.
This vote saw the biggest failed money play in US campaign history with Elon Musk spending a reported $US450m ($650m) – the largest-ever single corporate spend – across a number of Republican candidates with a priority on Texas where his rejection was conspicuous and significant. Musk wasn’t alone since Silicon Valley tech bosses totalled more than $US600m in their doomed bid to keep AI data centres free from public constraints and guardrails.
Trump’s alignment with Big Tech has been a disastrous political negative. It both split his MAGA base and alienated much of the centrist vote. MAGA luminary Steve Bannon had previously declared AI to be “the most dangerous technology in the history of mankind” but Trump climbed aboard, declared dire warnings about AI were a “hoax”, seized 10 per cent of semiconductor company Intel, and established a close, deal-making intimacy with Nvidia boss Jensen Huang, who now admits to an affair with a woman suspected of being a Chinese spy.
Texas, location of Musk’s company, is aligned with about a quarter of planned data centres in the US but saw a Republican wipeout in a huge spending contest. Trump-backed Republican Ken Paxton was defeated for the Senate seat by Democrat James Talarico, the first time the party has won a Senate seat in Texas in nearly 40 years.
In his victory speech, Talarico declared a turning point: “We just proved that all the money in the world is no match for the people of Texas. We just showed that a politics of division is no match for a politics of love.” Talarico campaigned against Big Tech, Trump’s corruption and the politics of hate, singling out “the billionaires who own the social media algorithms” and “the richest man in the world” for seeking to control the ecosystem. At the same time, Texas Republican Governor Greg Abbott lost to Democrat Gina Hinojosa, who wants a moratorium on data centres until legal protections are enacted.
Democrat Governor of Pennsylvania, Josh Shapiro, said: “We made sure that Big Tech doesn’t get to write the rules that shape our future, but instead the folks in our local communities get the final say.” Democrat senator Mark Warner said that while data centres and AI offered possibilities for innovation and creation, they were “too important to be left to Donald Trump and a few of these tech bros making all the rules”.
With the Democrats controlling the congress, the future points to a slowdown in data centre growth, more legislated checks and protections, more congressional inquiry into the tech companies, and rising criticism of the AI giants for abusing excessive power in their financial interests. Wall Street can see the trend and knows a slowdown is coming. After this electoral savaging, many Republicans will be wary of being tied politically to Big Tech and the data centre push – though Trump is unlikely to be swayed.
The alliance between Trump, Big Tech and Big Money to minimise controls and safety has backfired spectacularly. The hostility is more to data centres than AI. The message is strong political support for data centre accountability. But AI will be subject to greater accountability in terms of jobs, copyright and protection of children, along with probing the special deals between AI chiefs and the Trump administration.
While left-wing Democrats will overreach, the crucial point remains: this is not a vote against AI. It is a vote to bring a democratic process to the AI revolution. Ultimately, it is in the interest of the industry given it needs a more solid financial foundation as investors have begun to ruthlessly cut overextended positions in the market.
With near perfect timing the Albanese government announced on Tuesday its safety and security protections for its AI standards legislation to build trust in frontier AI and deliver its so-called social licence. The message: AI is no “free-for-all” in Australia but will come with firm guardrails. Yet reconciling both effective public protections and a strong AI expansion into this country – seen by Labor as essential to lift our productivity and living standards – is a combination that challenges our real-world capabilities.
Above all, as Assistant Minister for Technology and the Digital Economy Andrew Charlton says, the acceptable test for data centres is ensuring power prices are not pushed up. Charlton wants Australia to learn from the US experience. He can double down on that.
But note Gillian Tett’s November 7 article in the Financial Times, “Why does America hate AI?” with its graph based on a Pew Research Centre 2026 global survey of industrialised nations showing degrees of concern and excitement about AI. Surprisingly, it shows Australia as the lead country in the “more concerned than excited” category about AI, just ahead of the US, the second-most concerned nation. Brazil, Canada, Italy and the UK follow in that order; the least concerned nations are South Korea, India, Turkey and Japan.
One message from Tett’s article is that governments need to run substantial and co-ordinated agendas on a large scale to address the structural and social transformations AI will bring, and get their publics to the stage where they see the benefits, not just the fears.
At the same time, Tett raises a profound question – yet to surface in Australia but inevitable in the future: How the Judaeo-Christian theology of humans possessing souls and therefore separate from machines will be challenged by the idea of humanoid robots and the notion that humanity will evolve and integrate with the technology.
Will AI be seen as external to or eventually internal to the self? Pope Leo in his recent encyclical sought to confront and answer this question by upholding the uniqueness of the human soul. Indeed, it is not an exaggeration to see the US vote as a practical defence of human agency, yet this question is destined to be addressed at both the economic and metaphysical level.
Shifting to the more mundane, governments in the US and Australia face the dual economic impact of AI – it is driving activity, investment and hoped-for productivity yet such activity is also risking higher inflation. How will this play out in Australia?
At her media conference last week, RBA governor Michele Bullock was asked the pivotal question: Given that higher productivity is the key to growth with lower inflation, when might AI deliver this benefit?
Bullock said: “Ultimately, if productivity improves dramatically because of AI, it’ll do a couple of things. One, obviously, it’ll allow us to grow faster. The other thing that’s happening is that because the demand for investment in AI is so big at the moment, it’s outstripping savings, and that’s leading to an increase in what we call the neutral interest rate. So if people think that productivity improvements will help to lower inflation and keep interest rates low, that’s not necessarily the case, because the neutral interest rate in these circumstances is likely to rise and, you know, arguably we’re seeing it rise around the world at the moment.” The message: the advance of AI comes with ongoing high interest rates while the actual benefits of AI are sure to be uneven across the workforce. The US vote shows what the public wants – but AI cannot be stopped and getting its regulation right is a task without precedent.
